facts.statement: Wapuskanectes is classified as a genus within the family Elasmosauridae.
The genus Wapuskanectes belongs to the family Elasmosauridae.
The genus Wapuskanectes was named by Druckenmiller and Russell in 2006.
Patrick S. Druckenmiller and Anthony P. Russell named the genus Wapuskanectes in 2006.
facts.quote: Wapuskanectes was named by Patrick S. Druckenmiller and Anthony P. Russell in 2006.

facts.statement: Wapuskanectes is the oldest known elasmosaurid in North America, dating to approximately 112 million years ago.
facts.quote: Wapuskanectes is the oldest North American elasmosaurid to date, at around 112 million years old.

facts.statement: Fossils of Wapuskanectes have been found in Alberta, Canada, within the Albian-aged Wabiskaw Member of the Clearwater Formation.
facts.quote: known from Alberta, Canada, in the Albian aged Wabiskaw member of the Clearwater Formation.

facts.statement: Wapuskanectes lived during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous, between 113.2 and 110.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Albian to Albian (113.2 to 110.1 million years ago)

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Wapuskanectes is an articulated partial postcranial skeleton that includes an almost complete pectoral girdle.
facts.quote: The holotype is TMP 98.49.02, an articulated partial postcranial skeleton including an almost complete pectoral girdle.

facts.statement: The holotype was collected from the western side of the Syncrude Base Mine near Fort McMurray.
facts.quote: It was collected in the western side of the Syncrude Canada Ltd.'s open-pit oilsand mine (Syncrude Base Mine) near Ft. McMurray

facts.statement: Gastroliths in one specimen were found poking out of the dorsal side between the ribs, indicating the animal rested on its back after death.
facts.quote: Gastroliths in TMP 2012.50.1 could be seen poking out of the dorsal side of the body between the ribs, as after death it had come to rest on the seabed on its back.

facts.statement: The gastroliths found in Wapuskanectes have a composition similar to early Aptian conglomerate rocks from the Cadomin Formation.
facts.quote: The gastroliths in both genera were found to have similar composition to the early Aptian aged conglomerate rocks in the Cadomin Formation

facts.statement: Researchers hypothesize that Wapuskanectes swam westward to collect gastroliths from eroding beaches and river mouths along the western coast of the Western Interior Seaway.
facts.quote: it is hypothesized that they may have swum westward from the northern Western Interior Seaway to collect the Cadomin rocks eroding out of the beaches and river mouths of the Seaway's western coast.

facts.statement: Despite being ten times heavier than the similar reptile Nichollsaura, Wapuskanectes carried gastroliths weighing five times as much.
facts.quote: despite Wapuskanectes having 10 times more mass than Nichollsaura. The former did have larger gastroliths and an estimated 5 times the weight in gastroliths however.

facts.statement: Several specimens of Wapuskanectes have been discovered, with the most complete found 30 km away from the original mine site.
facts.quote: Several specimens have been discovered, the most complete of which is TMP 2012.50.1, found 30 km away from the Syncrude mine where previous specimens were found.

facts.statement: The most complete specimen was discovered when heavy machinery ploughed through the fossil, destroying the skull and most of the neck.
facts.quote: It was discovered when a grader ploughed through the neck, resulting in the destruction of the skull and most of the neck.

facts.statement: The specific name 'nectes' in the genus name comes from the Greek word for 'swimmer'.
The species name honors the late Dr. Elizabeth 'Betsy' Nicholls, a curator at the Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology, for her lasting influence on Mesozoic marine vertebrate research.
facts.quote: El nombre de la especie es en homenaje a la difunta Dra. Elizabeth "Betsy" Nicholls, curadora de reptiles marinos en el Real Museo Tyrrell de Paleontología, por su perdurable influencia en la investigación de los vertebrados marinos del Mesozoico.
